analysis.one_liner: Imposes an excise tax on large corporations whose CEO pay is more than 50 times worker pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its first referral; no committee vote or House floor vote was ever held in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a tax on very large companies—those with at least $100 million in annual gross receipts and $10 million in annual payroll—if their top executive's pay is more than 50 times the pay of the typical employee. The tax grows with the size of the pay gap, but is capped at 1% of the company's gross receipts. It was introduced in the House in November 2023 and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which took no further action before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary employees at the very largest corporations benefit indirectly: the tax is designed to pressure companies to narrow CEO-to-worker pay gaps, either by raising median worker pay or restraining executive compensation. The revenue from the tax would go to the federal government rather than directly to workers.

how_it_helps.text: Applies only to large employers with at least $100 million in annual gross receipts and $10 million in annual payroll for three consecutive years, so small and midsize businesses are untouched.
The tax rises with the size of the pay disparity: it equals 1% of gross receipts times the amount by which the CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio exceeds 50, capped at 1% of gross receipts.
The bill directs the Treasury Department to write regulations preventing companies from gaming the ratio, including by replacing employees with contractors.

The tax amount is not deductible from corporate income taxes, and the bill includes joint-and-several liability for companies treated as a single employer under an aggregation rule, to prevent corporate restructuring from evading the tax.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations—roughly the biggest 1,000 or so firms by size—that pay their chief executives more than 50 times their median worker's pay. The cost falls on the company, not on executives personally, and could be passed to shareholders or, in some cases, workers through reduced compensation budgets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large companies with high pay ratios

drawbacks.text: The bill taxes the company rather than paying workers directly: nothing in the bill requires a company to raise median wages; it may instead choose to absorb the tax, trim executive pay, or pass costs to shareholders.

The pay ratio could be manipulated by shifting work to contractors or staffing firms; the bill directs Treasury to write anti-avoidance regulations, but the safeguards depend on future rules that did not exist in the bill text.

The tax applies even when a company's pay ratio is driven by an unusually low-paid median employee rather than an unusually high CEO, so firms with modest executive pay but low-wage workforces could still owe the tax.
Compliance would require each covered firm to compute a five-year average CEO pay figure and a median wage annually, adding tax-compliance work on top of the existing SEC pay-ratio disclosures.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a blunt instrument: it does not guarantee any worker gets a raise, and a company could pay the tax rather than change its pay structure. But it is deliberately narrow—aimed only at very large firms with extreme pay gaps—and includes anti-avoidance rules for the most predictable workarounds like contractor substitution. The realistic best-case outcome is modest pressure toward either raising median pay or curbing executive compensation at the largest firms; the realistic worst case is a compliance burden with little behavioral change. The bill's practical significance is limited by the fact that it never received any committee or floor action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Barbara Lee introduced the Curtailing Executive Overcompensation (CEO) Act in the House on November 2, 2023, with six original cosponsors including Ocasio-Cortez, Frost, Norton, Tlaib, Jackson Lee, Jayapal, and Bowman.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction, and the public record shows no further action—not a hearing, not a markup, not a floor vote—for the remainder of the 118th Congress.
All 11 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and no companion measure advanced in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with high CEO-to-worker pay ratios benefit, since no tax or disclosure pressure was ever enacted. Their chief executives' compensation levels remain untouched by law. The Ways and Means Committee's inaction also preserved the status quo for its members' large corporate constituents without any recorded vote on the merits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations with high pay ratios

industries.industry: Large corporations with high CEO-to-worker pay ratios (retail, tech, hospitality, finance)
industries.note: These firms would owe an excise tax of up to 1% of gross receipts whenever their executive-to-median-worker pay ratio exceeds 50 to 1. Their interest is to keep the status quo, which conflicts with the bill's aim of narrowing pay gaps—though workers benefit only indirectly, since the bill does not mandate any pay change.

industries.industry: Executive compensation consultants and pay-ratio compliance advisors
industries.note: Firms would need to compute and document the new pay disparity factor each year, creating a compliance services market. This cost exists only if the bill passes; it died.

The bill explicitly targets contractor substitution as a way to game the pay ratio, signaling that companies might otherwise shift low-wage work to contractors. The bill's regulations would police this practice.
